<reason>This was an unusually even, sharp exchange. Both sides held coherent frameworks and traded real blows. B's best live routes were the dual-party "demolition" arithmetic, the incumbent-grandfathering asymmetry ("amnesty with a moat"), and the smart-reply/provider-exception point showing A's purpose-and-beneficiary line requires exactly the downstream judgment B's regime supplies. A blunted the demolition via de-identification and an orphan-works style exception, reframed the asymmetry as the motion's purpose rather than its flaw, and answered smart replies by noting platforms can ask their users. A's decisive edge was the irreversibility/unverifiability attack: every remedy B offered (deletion, correction, retraining) arrives after training, when no one can verify what the weights have forgotten, and B never answered that squarely. A also crisply resolved both pressure questions with the required A1/A2 structure and kept the clash narrow across rounds. B's execution costs — a clipped opening and a clipped rebuttal 2 — cost a final beat in two of its strongest speeches. Narrow but real edge to PRO on the motion as written.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The smart-reply/provider-exception exchange (B4.7 vs A5.4) and the verifiability clash (B4.3 vs A5.2). B landed the strongest structural hit by showing spam-filter and smart-reply training fall inside A's own provider-exception logic, forcing A into purpose judgments that mirror B's regime; A's reply that platforms with user relationships can simply ask was glib and left the two-party tension dangling. But A's counter on remedial unverifiability — that deletion and retraining obligations against model weights cannot be checked after the fact, making B's regime "a promise made by the taker after the taking" — was the single most damaging unresolved blow of the debate.</best_rebuttal>
